title: Collibra UX pattern catalog
implementation_boundary: This is a framework-neutral interaction contract. Product teams own service behavior, data rules, and runtime implementation.
principles: Orient before asking the user to act.
Make system state visible and recoverable.
Prefer progressive disclosure over hidden complexity.
Keep primary actions and consequences explicit.
Treat keyboard, assistive technology, and constrained viewports as first-class paths.
Separate generated suggestions from confirmed records or decisions.
Show provenance and uncertainty when they affect a decision.
Measure the task outcome before adding automation or complexity.

patterns.name: Workspace shell
patterns.goal: Give users a stable sense of location, scope, current work, and next action across a multi-surface product.
when: The product has more than one context or workflow.
Users need to return to a parent context after inspecting detail.
flow: Establish product and workspace context.
Show current location and active scope.
Expose the primary task path.
Keep secondary navigation available without competing with the task.
Preserve context after refresh, error, or return from detail.

resilience.loading: Keep the shell and location visible while local content loads.
resilience.empty: Explain which scope is empty and give one relevant next action.
resilience.error: Keep navigation usable and place recovery next to the failed surface.

accessibility: Use landmarks and a consistent heading hierarchy.
Keep current location and selected navigation state programmatically exposed.
Do not require hover to discover navigation.
content: Use user-facing names for workspaces and resources.
Make active scope visible before actions that depend on it.
Keep navigation labels parallel and concise.
safety: Do not hide permission or data-scope boundaries in navigation.
Do not make a destructive action the only global action.
anti_patterns: A shell that changes structure between pages without explanation.
A global menu that hides the current location.
A loading screen that removes the route back to safety.
patterns.success: A user can state where they are, what scope they are in, and how to start or resume the current task.

patterns.name: Search and filter discovery
patterns.goal: Help users find the right records without losing their query, scope, or understanding of why results changed.
when: The result set is larger than a user can scan.
Users need to combine free-text search with known facets or attributes.
flow: Show the active scope and query context.
Accept a query or filter change.
Show which filters are active.
Update results with a visible status.
Offer clear removal, reset, and no-match recovery.

resilience.loading: Keep the query and active filters visible while results update.
resilience.empty: Distinguish no records in scope from no matches for the current query.
resilience.error: Preserve the query and offer retry or a narrower scope without silently resetting the form.

accessibility: Expose active filters and result count or status in text.
Keep focus in the input or filter control that initiated an update.
Make filter removal controls individually named.
content: Name the field or facet in user language.
Explain why no results were found and what to try next.
Use stable units, date formats, and capitalization in result labels.
safety: Do not broaden the scope silently when a query returns no results.
Do not treat search relevance as proof of authority or correctness.
anti_patterns: Filters that disappear when a result loads.
A no-results message that implies the record does not exist.
Search that changes scope without a visible boundary.
patterns.success: A user can reproduce the current result set from the visible query, filters, and scope.

patterns.name: List and detail inspection
patterns.goal: Support scanning a collection and inspecting one item without losing position, query context, or a route back.
when: Users compare multiple records and occasionally need deeper detail.
Detail is contextual rather than a separate workflow.
flow: Present a scannable collection.
Make the selected item and available actions explicit.
Open detail in a drawer or dedicated route according to task complexity.
Keep the source context and selection visible.
Return to the same collection position after close or save.

resilience.loading: Keep the collection structure visible and avoid changing selection while detail loads.
resilience.empty: Explain whether the collection or only the current scope is empty.
resilience.error: Keep the collection usable if detail fails and offer a direct retry.

accessibility: Use headings and table or list semantics that match the data.
Move focus deliberately into detail and return it to the invoking item.
Expose selection and expanded detail state.
content: Lead detail with the identity and purpose of the item.
Use the same names in collection and detail.
Separate facts, actions, history, and related context.
safety: Do not make inspecting an item mutate it.
Show which record and scope an action will affect before submission.
anti_patterns: Detail that opens with no visible relationship to the selected row.
A drawer that contains an entire unrelated workflow.
Returning to the first page after closing detail.
patterns.success: A user can inspect an item, understand its context, and return to the same place in the collection.

patterns.name: Command and quick action surface
patterns.goal: Make frequent actions discoverable and fast without turning the product into an opaque command language.
when: Experienced users repeat a small set of cross-context actions.
The product has a stable action vocabulary and visible scope.
flow: Open from a labeled, discoverable trigger.
Search or browse available actions.
Show the active scope and any required inputs.
Preview material consequences.
Confirm, complete, or recover without losing the source context.

resilience.loading: Keep the trigger and scope visible while actions are being resolved.
resilience.empty: Explain that no action matches the query and show the available scope or recovery path.
resilience.error: Keep the source task intact and explain whether the action ran, failed, or was not started.

accessibility: Use a named trigger and predictable keyboard navigation.
Do not require memorized shortcuts for essential actions.
Expose scope and confirmation content before execution.
content: Use the same action verbs as visible buttons.
Show required parameters in plain language.
Name irreversible or broad effects before confirmation.
safety: Keep the command surface read-only until the user explicitly confirms a material action.
Do not hide permission boundaries or active scope.
anti_patterns: A command palette that exposes actions a user cannot perform.
Shortcuts that silently act on the wrong scope.
Commands that replace visible recovery paths.
patterns.success: A user can discover a frequent action, see what it will affect, and execute or cancel it confidently.

patterns.name: Create and edit form
patterns.goal: Collect or revise structured values with clear constraints, preserved input, and an explicit completion boundary.
when: The user must provide several related values.
The outcome is durable or needs validation before commit.
flow: Explain the object or decision being edited.
Group fields in the user's task order.
Show constraints before or at entry.
Validate without destroying input.
Save explicitly and confirm the resulting state.

resilience.loading: Show which fields or related values are still loading without blocking independent entry.
resilience.empty: Explain when a required option set is empty and who can resolve it.
resilience.error: Preserve all recoverable input and identify the field or service that needs attention.

accessibility: Associate labels, descriptions, required state, and errors with each control.
Keep validation announcements useful without moving focus unpredictably.
Use native control semantics where possible.
content: Use labels that describe the value.
Explain constraints in advance.
Use errors that state the fix, not just that the value is invalid.
safety: Make save and cancel outcomes explicit.
Confirm before discarding material unsaved work.
Do not use an immediate switch for an irreversible change.
anti_patterns: Placeholder-only labels.
A form that reports success before persistence is confirmed.
A save failure that clears the form.
patterns.success: A user can complete or cancel the form and knows whether the intended change is durable.

patterns.name: Structured data review
patterns.goal: Help users compare, inspect, and decide on structured information without losing provenance or change context.
when: A decision depends on multiple records, fields, or event history.
The product needs a human review boundary before committing a change.
flow: Declare the review scope and source.
Present a scannable summary.
Allow focused inspection and filtering.
Show differences, missing evidence, and unresolved issues.
Commit a decision or leave the review explicitly incomplete.

resilience.loading: Show the review scope and source while individual data regions load.
resilience.empty: Distinguish no data from no evidence for the chosen scope.
resilience.error: Mark incomplete regions and keep already loaded evidence inspectable.

accessibility: Expose row, column, tree, timeline, and diff relationships in the chosen structure.
Make selected changes and unresolved items available as text.
Do not make color highlighting the only difference cue.
content: Name the source and review date when known.
Separate confirmed, proposed, missing, and conflicting information.
Use stable labels across summary and detail.
safety: Do not convert a missing source into a negative finding.
Require an explicit boundary before applying reviewed changes.
Keep the original value available during review.
anti_patterns: A dashboard that hides the records behind unexplained scores.
An accepted change with no visible review history.
Treating retrieved evidence as automatically authoritative.
patterns.success: A reviewer can explain what was examined, what remains uncertain, and what decision was actually made.

patterns.name: AI assist and human review
patterns.goal: Let users get useful assistance while keeping scope, provenance, uncertainty, and human control visible.
when: Generated content or suggested changes can accelerate a user task.
The user must remain accountable for a decision or durable change.
flow: Show the active scope and available assistant capability.
Collect the request with inspectable context.
Show generation state and partial or failed output honestly.
Separate answer, assumptions, sources, and suggested actions.
Require review before a durable or material change.
Confirm the result and preserve a recovery path.

resilience.loading: Show what is being generated and keep stop or cancel available.
resilience.empty: Explain when no source context or result is available instead of fabricating a response.
resilience.error: Keep the request and partial output inspectable and state whether retry is safe.

accessibility: Announce meaningful lifecycle changes without repeatedly stealing focus.
Make generated, cited, proposed, and confirmed content distinguishable in text.
Expose all review actions to keyboard and assistive technology.
content: Label generated content as generated.
State uncertainty and source limitations when they affect use.
Use explicit verbs for accept, reject, retry, stop, and apply.
safety: No silent durable writes.
No hidden scope expansion or tool use.
No claim of certainty or authority that the evidence does not support.
anti_patterns: A chat transcript that hides the active data scope.
An answer that looks like a confirmed record.
A generated change applied without review or undo.
patterns.success: A user can say what the assistant saw, what it suggested, what evidence it had, and what the user chose to do.

patterns.name: Long-running operation
patterns.goal: Keep an asynchronous task understandable, stoppable, and recoverable without forcing the user to wait on a frozen surface.
when: An operation can outlast the current interaction.
The user needs to continue other work while a task runs.
flow: Name the operation and active scope.
Show queued, running, paused, or blocked state.
Expose progress or honest indeterminate status.
Offer stop, pause, retry, or details when supported.
Show completion, partial result, failure, or cancellation explicitly.

resilience.loading: Use a stable operation name and state rather than an unexplained spinner.
resilience.empty: Explain when an operation completed without producing a result.
resilience.error: State whether retry will duplicate work, resume safely, or require a new request.

accessibility: Announce meaningful transitions at a useful rate.
Expose stop and retry controls with clear names.
Do not require the user to monitor animation to know that work continues.
content: Name what is happening now.
Use complete, partial, failed, and canceled language precisely.
Tell the user what remains to be done.
safety: Make stop semantics explicit.
Do not report completion before the output is available or verified.
Do not retry a non-idempotent operation without a clear boundary.
anti_patterns: A permanent progress indicator with no timeout or recovery.
A completion toast that cannot be inspected later.
A retry that silently starts duplicate work.
patterns.success: A user can leave and return to the operation and still understand its state, result, and next safe action.

patterns.name: Error and recovery
patterns.goal: Turn failure into an understandable, local, recoverable state without blaming the user or losing their work.
when: A request, field, data region, or background operation can fail.
The user needs to decide whether to retry, change input, or ask for help.
flow: Keep the user's context and input.
State what failed and where.
Separate known facts from unknown cause.
Offer the smallest useful recovery action.
Confirm whether recovery worked or whether the task remains blocked.

resilience.loading: Label a retry in progress and keep the failed context visible.
resilience.empty: Do not use an error state for expected absence; explain the actual scope instead.
resilience.error: Name the recovery action, preserve input, and state what remains unavailable.

accessibility: Use text and semantics for error state, not color alone.
Associate field errors with their controls.
Do not move focus to a distant banner without a clear reason.
content: Say what happened in user terms.
Say what the user can do next.
Avoid fabricated causes or blame.
safety: Do not retry automatically when it could duplicate a material action.
Do not reveal secrets or sensitive implementation detail in an error.
Keep partial results marked as partial.
anti_patterns: Something went wrong with no recovery path.
Clearing user input after an error.
A success message that masks a partial failure.
patterns.success: A user can distinguish failed, incomplete, unavailable, and recovered states and knows the next safe action.

patterns.name: Destructive confirmation
patterns.goal: Prevent accidental irreversible or high-impact actions while keeping deliberate work efficient.
when: The action is destructive, broad, irreversible, or difficult to undo.
The consequence would surprise a reasonable user from the visible action label alone.
flow: Name the exact object, scope, and consequence.
Ask for an explicit decision.
Use an action label that names the consequence.
Complete or cancel without ambiguity.
Show the resulting state and recovery path when one exists.

resilience.loading: Keep the exact scope and action visible while submission is in progress.
resilience.empty: Do not show a confirmation when there is no target or no action to perform.
resilience.error: State whether the action happened, did not happen, or is uncertain; do not claim safe rollback without evidence.

accessibility: Give the dialog a title and description that name the consequence.
Keep focus within the confirmation and return it to the trigger on cancel.
Make the confirm and cancel actions distinct in text.
content: Name the object and scope.
Use the irreversible verb in the confirm action.
Explain undo or lack of undo.
safety: Require explicit confirmation for material impact.
Never rely on color or position alone to signal danger.
Do not change the target while the dialog is open.
anti_patterns: Generic Confirm labels.
A confirmation that omits the target or consequence.
Using confirmation as a substitute for a safe default or undo.
patterns.success: A user can state what will happen before confirming and can tell what happened afterward.

patterns.name: First-use and no-content state
patterns.goal: Help users understand an expected absence of records or setup and take the smallest useful next step.
when: The user has no records yet.
The current scope, filter, or permission produces no visible content.
flow: Name the current scope.
Classify the absence as first use, no matches, unavailable, or not permitted.
Explain the next step in one sentence.
Offer one relevant setup, reset, request, or return action.
Preserve context after the action.

resilience.loading: Keep the scope and expected content shape visible while the first load resolves.
resilience.empty: Explain the specific kind of absence instead of presenting a generic blank surface.
resilience.error: Distinguish no data from failed retrieval and offer a safe recovery path.

accessibility: Expose the reason for absence in text.
Make the next action keyboard reachable.
Do not use decorative illustration as the only explanation.
content: Use a calm, factual explanation.
Offer one next action rather than a list of unrelated possibilities.
Avoid implying that missing data is a user mistake.
safety: Do not fabricate sample records that could be mistaken for real data.
Do not broaden scope to make the surface look populated.
Respect permission boundaries in the explanation.
anti_patterns: An empty white surface with no explanation.
Sample content that looks live.
A setup action that changes scope without telling the user.
patterns.success: A user knows why the surface is empty and what one safe next action is available.

patterns.name: Responsive and adaptive layout
patterns.goal: Preserve task hierarchy, meaning, and control access when the available viewport or input mode changes.
when: A surface can be used at different viewport sizes or with different input modes.
Dense data or secondary detail needs a different presentation at constrained sizes.
flow: Identify the primary task and required controls.
Keep critical identity, status, and action information visible.
Move secondary detail into an explicit disclosure or drawer.
Preserve reading order, focus, and state across layout changes.
Test the constrained path with keyboard and assistive technology.

resilience.loading: Preserve the same loading meaning and operation label across layouts.
resilience.empty: Keep the reason and next action visible after reflow.
resilience.error: Keep the failed context and recovery action reachable without relying on a hover or hidden overflow.

accessibility: Preserve semantic order even when visual order changes.
Keep focus on the same logical item after reflow.
Make horizontal overflow intentional, labeled, and keyboard usable.
content: Shorten labels only when the meaning stays intact.
Prefer disclosure over truncation for identity and decision-critical values.
Keep action labels explicit in every layout.
safety: Do not hide destructive or required actions only because space is constrained.
Do not change the active scope during reflow.
Do not turn data relationships into unexplained visual cards.
anti_patterns: A mobile layout that removes the current identity or status.
A table that becomes unreadable cards with no relationship cues.
An overflow menu that contains the only recovery action.
patterns.success: A user can complete the same core task and understand the same state at every supported layout.

patterns.name: Inspectable provenance
patterns.goal: Make the source, freshness, status, and limits of information visible when a user must trust or review it.
when: A result is generated, aggregated, imported, or derived.
A decision depends on evidence that can be missing, stale, partial, or conflicting.
flow: State what the information represents.
Show source or provenance affordance near the relevant claim.
Expose date, status, and limitations when known.
Separate source evidence from interpretation or suggestion.
Allow the user to inspect the underlying context.

resilience.loading: Show that provenance is still resolving and do not imply completeness.
resilience.empty: State when no source evidence is available.
resilience.error: Keep the claim marked as unsupported or incomplete and explain the inspection failure.

accessibility: Expose provenance labels, dates, and status as text.
Make the inspection path keyboard reachable.
Do not require color or an icon to distinguish source from interpretation.
content: Use source names users can recognize.
Distinguish sourced, inferred, proposed, and unknown content.
Use absolute dates when freshness matters.
safety: Never invent a source or freshness signal.
Do not present retrieval as validation.
Keep missing evidence visible when it affects a decision.
anti_patterns: A citation marker with no inspectable source.
A freshness badge with no date or rule.
A generated summary that hides conflicting evidence.
patterns.success: A user can tell what is known, where it came from, how current it is, and what remains uncertain.
